EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine Learning Data is the fuel that powers machine learning algorithms. Without data, these algorithms cannot learn patterns, make predictions, or improve over time. 29
EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine Learning The quality, quantity, and relevance of the data directly influence the performance of machine learning models. 30

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine LearningData Quality Accuracy of Predictions: When the data is clean, relevant, and representative of the problem domain, the model can learn effectively and make reliable predictions. Robustness: Models trained on high-quality data can generalize better to unseen data, which is crucial for real-world applications. Bias Reduction: Poor data quality can introduce biases that skew the model's predictions. Interpretability: Stakeholders can
quality can introduce biases that skew the model's predictions. Interpretability: Stakeholders can understand how and why certain predictions are made, fostering trust in the model. 31

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine LearningData Quantity For a machine learning model to learn, it has to be exposed to data during the “learning” or “training” phase. However, we can’t feed a model all existing data about a topic, so we take a subset that is called a ‘training set’. This training set, while a smaller version, should encapsulate the diversity and patterns present in the general population. 32

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine LearningData Quantity Having a large and diverse dataset can enhance learning and generalization. Data scarcity causes multiple problems which include: 1. Lack of generalizability. 2. Low accuracy. 3. Mismatch between model complexity and data size. 33

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Role of Data in Machine LearningData Relevance Data relevance refers to the degree to which the data used in training a machine learning model is applicable to the problem being solved. Relevant data helps in capturing the underlying patterns and relationships that the model needs to learn. When data is relevant, it enhances the model's ability to generalize well to unseen data, thereby improving its predictive performance. 34

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data To understand how to represent an image in a numerical format, we need to understand what makes an image. The smallest building block of an image is called a pixel. 57

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data The size of an image is described by the number of pixels in the height and the width. Example: 1920x1080. This means that the screen will have a width of 1,920 pixels while the height of the screen will be 1,080 pixels. This results in a grand total of 2,073,600 pixels on-screen. Each pixel has an intensity value that describes the intensity of color at that pixel. 58

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data 59 The matrix of pixel intensities in an image is used as a numeric representation of that image. The range of an image’s pixel intensity depends on the image type. We will go through the main image types: Black and white, Grayscale, RGB, RGBA, Multi-Spectral, and Depth Maps

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Manipulating Image Data: OpenCV Library To visualize the pixel values, we will use the opencv library to load the image and print its values. For readability, we will resize the images to a smaller size. 60
EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data Black and white images: Pixels are either 0 (black) or 1 (white), representing a binary image. 61

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data Grayscale Images: Pixel values range from 0 (black) to 255 (white) for 8-bit images. Higher bit-depth grayscale images (e.g., 16-bit) extend this range. 62

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data RGB images: each pixel in an RGB image can be represented as three values: Red, Green, and Blue. Thus, RGB images can be represented as three channels. Each channel represents one red, green, and blue intensities respectively. 63

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data RGBA images: Similar to RGB but with an additional alpha channel for transparency, where the alpha value typically ranges from 0 (fully transparent) to 255 (fully opaque). 64

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data Multi-Spectral images: Images captured across multiple wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum, typically beyond the standard visible light range (red, green, and blue). Commonly include 4–12 spectral bands, compared to the 3 bands (RGB) in standard images. Examples: Visible (RGB), near-infrared (NIR), short-wave infrared (SWIR), and ultraviolet (UV). 65

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation of Image Data Depth Maps: A representation of the distances between the camera (or sensor) and objects in a scene, where each pixel's value corresponds to the depth (or distance) of that point. These maps are typically grayscale images where brighter pixels represent objects closer to the camera, and darker pixels represent objects farther away. 66

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation: Audio & Time Series Data Sliding Window: An approach used to capture discrete instances of continuous data that can be used for image or tabular transformation. After segmenting the data into windows, a ‘window function’ is applied to each segment to reduce the edge effects (discontinuities) that would otherwise be introduced by dividing the signal into chunks. 69

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Numerical Representation: Audio & Time Series Data A window function is a mathematical function that is applied to each segment of the audio signal before performing any analysis (like Fourier Transform). The purpose of the window function is to smooth the signal at the edges of each segment, reducing the abrupt discontinuities. This minimizes the spectral leakage (energy spreading into other frequency bins) that results from discontinuities at the edges of the
(energy spreading into other frequency bins) that results from discontinuities at the edges of the windows. 70

EECE 490: Introduction to ML 83 Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) 1. Initialize the text sequence ○ Example: "banana" → b a n a n a 2. Identify the most frequent adjacent pair ○ The pair "a n" appears most frequently. 3. Merge the selected pair ○ Updated sequence: b AN a n a 4. Repeat the merging process ○ Final sequence: b AN AN a Result: The text is tokenized into fewer subword units, reducing vocabulary size while preserving structure.

EECE 490: Introduction to ML 84 WordPiece Tokenization 1. Input word: "unhappiness" 1. Split into subwords: ["un", "happiness"] 1. Check vocabulary: If "happiness" is not found, split further. 1. Select tokens: ["un", "happi", "##ness"] ("##" indicates a continuation). 1. Final tokens: ["un", "happi", "##ness"], reducing vocabulary size while preserving meaning.

EECE 490: Introduction to ML 85 BERT Tokenization Input Sentence: "Playing outside is fun." Step 1: Apply WordPiece Tokenization ● "Playing" → ["Play", "##ing"] (split into subwords) ● "outside" → ["outside"] (kept as is) ● "is" → ["is"] (kept as is) ● "fun" → ["fun"] (kept as is) Step 2: Add Special Tokens ● [CLS] at the beginning ● [SEP] at the end Final Tokenized Output: ["[CLS]", "Play", "##ing", "outside", "is", "fun", "[SEP]"]

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics Clustering evaluation metrics are generally divided into internal and external measures. 37

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - Internal Metrics These metrics evaluate the quality of the clusters based solely on the data that was clustered. 1. Silhouette Score: Measures the degree of separation between clusters. How It’s Computed: For each data point, compute the difference between the average distance to points in the same cluster (cohesion) and the average distance to points in the nearest neighboring cluster (separation), then normalize this difference. 38

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - Internal Metrics Scores range from -1 to 1. A score near +1 indicates that the data point is well matched to its own cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters; a score near 0 indicates overlapping clusters; and negative values indicate that the point may have been assigned to the wrong cluster. 39

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - Internal Metrics 2. Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI): It is calculated as the average similarity measure of each cluster with the cluster most similar to it. In this context, similarity is defined as the ratio between inter-cluster and intra-cluster distances. As such, this index ranks well-separated clusters with less dispersion as having a better score. Interpretation: Lower values indicate better clustering because clusters are compact
better score. Interpretation: Lower values indicate better clustering because clusters are compact and distinct from each other. 40

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - Internal Metrics 3. Dunn Index: The ratio between the smallest distance between observations not in the same cluster (inter-cluster distance) and the largest intra-cluster distance. Interpretation: A higher Dunn index indicates better clustering with well-separated clusters. 41

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - External Metrics When true labels or a reference clustering is available, external metrics can quantify how well the clustering algorithm recovered the known structure. 1. Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): Similarity between the predicted clusters and the true labels, adjusted for chance. Interpretation: Scores range from -1 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect agreement. 42

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Clustering Evaluation Metrics - External Metrics 2. Normalized Mutual Information (NMI): The mutual dependence between the true labels and the predicted clusters, normalized to range between 0 and 1. Interpretation: Higher values indicate better alignment between the clusters and the true classes. 43

EECE 490: Introduction to ML What is the Null Hypothesis (H₀) In statistics (and by extension in ML), the null hypothesis is the idea that nothing special is happening. It’s a default assumption that there’s no effect, no difference, or no relationship between variables. Example: Let’s say you’re testing if a new model performs better than the old one. ● H₀ (null hypothesis): The new model performs the same as the old one (no improvement). ● H₁ (alternative hypothesis): The new model performs

the same as the old one (no improvement). ● H₁ (alternative hypothesis): The new model performs better than the old one. You start by assuming the null hypothesis is true until you find enough evidence (data) to reject it. 53

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Why it matters in ML In ML, you often compare models or evaluate features. For example: ● Is Model B’s accuracy truly higher than Model A’s, or is it just random noise? ● Does a specific feature really improve prediction, or not? Hypothesis testing helps you avoid overclaiming. You don’t want to say “the model improved” when, statistically, it might not have. 54

EECE 490: Introduction to ML What is a Z-score? The Z-score tells you how far a data point is from the average, measured in units of standard deviation. 56

EECE 490: Introduction to ML What is a Z-score? Example: If your model accuracy is 0.82, the average accuracy of similar models is 0.75, and the standard deviation is 0.05: That means your result is 1.4 standard deviations above the mean. 57

EECE 490: Introduction to ML How Z-score connects to hypothesis testing The Z-score helps you decide how unlikely your result is under the null hypothesis. If the Z-score is very large (say, greater than 1.96 or less than -1.96), your result is in the rare part of the distribution (only 5% of cases). That means it’s unlikely to happen by chance → you reject the null hypothesis. In ML terms: your model’s improvement is statistically significant. 58

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Regularization ● To reach an optimal model that does not overﬁt, we need to add a term to the cost function that ensures our model will have optimum complexity.

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Intuition behind Regularization Minimizing the old cost function leads to minimize the error only Minimizing the new cost function leads to minimize the error and the complexity ● The concept remains the same: We want to minimize the cost function. EECE 490: Introduction to ML How to measure complexity? ● One of the common things that reﬂect the complexity of a model is the number of features (consequently, parameters) that we have. ● As we increase those features, the chance of overﬁtting becomes more important. Thus we can either: - Reduce The Number of Features - Keep all the features and apply regularization

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Regularization ● Think of regularization as a way to keep all the features but prevent their importance from being large. ● Feature Importance is reﬂected by the values of their coefﬁcients. ● The complexity term to be minimized should thus reﬂect these values.

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Regularization Let’s say we need to minimize the effect of the feature x2 by reducing the corresponding parameter a2. One good thing to do to modify the cost function is something along the following lines: Multiply a2 by a large number Minimizing the cost would lead to minimizing the value of a2 since it’s multiplied by a large number, and thus we reduce the importance of x2 without removing it!

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Regularization – Ridge (L2) ● Suppose we have a model with p parameters. ● The complexity term is reﬂected by the squared sum of the p parameters multiplied by a regularization factor - Lambda. ● The Lambda (Regularization factor) penalizes large parameter values.

EECE 490: Introduction to ML Regularization – Lasso (L1) ● Suppose we have a model with p parameters ● The complexity term is reﬂected by the sum of the absolute value of the p parameters multiplied by a regularization factor - Lambda. ● The Lambda (Regularization factor) factor penalizes large parameter values.
